Women and girls in Somalia continue to experience heightened exposure and safety risks to Gender Based 
Violence as the first quarter of 2026 unfolds. Conflict, climate displacement have created a challenging 
environment, particularly in high-density Internally Displaced Population (IDP) hubs and conflict affected 
districts including Banadir (Daynile and Kahda), Lower Juba (Kismayo and Afmadow), Gedo (Doolow, 
Luuq, Belet Xaawo, Garbahaarey, Baardheere, and Ceel Waaq), Bay (Baidoa, Qansax Dheere, Hudur, and 
Diinsoor), Mudug (Hobyo, South Galkacyo, and Jariban), and Hiraan and Middle Shebelle (Belet Weyne, 
Jowhar, Adan Yabaal, Mahaday, Balcad, and Cadale).1

The 2026 Talk to Loop Report highlighted a significant number of cases (Protection and GBV) across 
several regions: Lower Shabelle (2,781); Galgaduud (220); Middle Shabelle (211); Hiraan (210); and Gedo 
(210). The surge in Lower Shabelle is primarily driven by the active military operations and clan-based 
insecurity, armed groups; and climate induced displacement in Afgoye and Bariire corridors. The data 
reveals how different groups experience or perceive harm. A total of 61 percent of women and girls 
reported direct physical safety threats, compared to (39 percent) of men and boys.2

The Gender Gap Analysis
Specific GBV Risks (OXFAM Analysis)
There is a stark “gendered divide” in how people experience systematic failure in the above regions. 
While women fear for their lives and bodies, men are more likely to report issues with the distribution 
of resources.
• Women & Girls (61 percent) of cases reported focuses on physical safety. This includes threats 
encountered while performing daily chores (collecting water/firewood) and risks within the home.
• Men & Boys (39 percent) of cases reported focuses on aid and services. This includes grievances 
regarding aid diversion and failures in how services are delivered.
Beyond the numbers, qualitative research 
from IDP sites in Baardheere, Beletweyne, 
and Laascaanod highlights three critical 
areas of concern:
• Domestic Threats: High prevalence 
of Intimate Partner Violence (IPV).
• Harmful Practices: A rise in early and 
forced marriages as a misguided 
coping mechanism.
• Environmental Risks: Women and girls 
are most vulnerable to harassment 
when walking to water points or 
traveling remote routes to collect 
firewood.

IPV remains the most prevalent form of GBV in both datasets, though the Luuq/Gedo district shows a 
higher concentration at 67 percent.
Both regional and national figures indicate that sexual violence accounts for roughly 1 in 7 reported 
cases, highlighting a critical need for continued protection service.
5
Gender Based Violence Situation -Ist Quarter 2026 
Specialized GBV services are currently in a state of crisis due to drastic funding cuts. Closures of GBV 
facilities including Women and girls’ safe spaces (WGSS) and GBV One stop centers (GBV OSCs); and 
the reduction of GBV service staff due to severity of funding gaps. These were primary inhibitors to 
access to service. 
Out of a total of 120 registered GBV centers, 66 (55%) are currently closed or non-operational. This includes 
Women and Girls’ Safe Spaces (WGSS) and One-Stop Centers (OSCs). In remote areas, the culture of 
silence persists not only due to stigma but due to the physical absence of any confidential reporting 
mechanism. The reduction in GBV specialized services is the most urgent barrier to survivor recovery.

The safety of women is heavily dictated by environmental factors and infrastructure. Below is the 
breakdown of reported safety concerns. The risk of GBV at night-time nearly doubles (from (36 percent) 
to (71 percent) once the sun sets. This directly correlates with the lack of energy infrastructure (solar

6
Gender Based Violence Situation -Ist Quarter 2026 
The Facility Crisis: A Statistical Breakdown
The HOD report on incidence of child and forced marriage is a major concern as child marriage provides 
conditions for exploitation and IPV - predisposing the child to increased future GBV risks. Economic 
vulnerability is the primary driver of IPV and Early Forced Marriage (50% incidence in HOD data).
Reports during the quarter four of 2025 and quarter one of 2026 identified groups most vulnerable to 
GBV risks to include: Adolescent girls, female headed households, minority clan women, persons with 
disabilities and newly displaced women and girls.

Key Challenges
• Massive funding cuts across the county have forced 55% of GBV facilities to close, leaving survivors 
with nowhere to go for confidential help.
• While cash assistance has helped, it is currently not enough to reach the vast number of women in 
need.
• Reporting of sexual harassment remains dangerously low because many survivors fear social stigma 
or do not know how to report safely.
7
Gender Based Violence Situation -Ist Quarter 2026 
Urgent action
• Well-lit and lockable latrines in IDP camps (WASH, Camp committees)
• Sustained use of cash assistance through case management to meet urgent needs (CASH ACTORS)
• Need to support the re-opening of women and girls’ safe spaces. (GBV Actors)
• Broader dissemination of PSEA messaging among key clusters (Food, WASH, Health)
Women and girls in Somalia remain at high risk of gender-based violence due to ongoing conflict, droughts 
floods and multiple displacements. While the 2026 Talk to the Loop report showed a high level of reported 
protection concerns, the actual capacity to help these survivors has been severely weakened. These 
risks are mainly due to food insecurity, and weak physical and economic security. 
 
Service limitation because of funding cuts and closure of GBV service sites impact on the ability of GBV 
survivors to access services. Increased response of cash assistance through case management in the 
4th quarter of 2025 and the first quarter 2026 improved GBV survivors’ ability to access services; however, 
this is still inadequate for the large population of women and girls with GBV, and protection needs. PSEA 
reporting is still low because of stigma, lack of confidence or ignorance of existing reporting channels.

GENEVA – Initial, on-the-ground needs assessments from Venezuela have revealed a dramatic surge in humanitarian and protection needs in recent days as teams evaluate the full impact of last week’s devastating earthquakes. In La Guaira – the hardest-hit state – food shortages are widespread, basic services have broken down, and connectivity has been largely severed. Community tensions are rising as access to assistance remains constrained. UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency, has immediately mobilized to support affected communities, and conducted a rapid needs assessment on 26-27 June with participants across La Guaira, the Capital District, Miranda, Aragua, and Carabobo states. The initial findings showed that: 75 per cent of respondents had reported injuries in their communities; 56 per cent reported fatalities. Older people and those with disabilities face compounded risks, due to limited mobility and reduced access to digital information. Further funding contributions are needed to enable the Cuban Red Cross, with the support of the IFRC, to continue to address the growing humanitarian needs of the communities affected by Hurricane Melissa in Cuba and the compounded effects of increasing health risks and persisting energy constraints.

The provinces of Guantánamo, Santiago de Cuba, Holguín, Granma, Las Tunas, and Camagüey were placed under the highest alert level, more than 735,000 peopl e were evacuated, and approximately 120,000 sought shelter in state facilities (United Nations System in Cuba, 2025).

Between 2019 and 2025, key health indicators have deteriorated: infant mortality increased from 5.0 to 9.9 per 1,000 live births; maternal mortality from 37.4 to 44.1 per 100,000 live births; and the low-birth-weight rate from 5.4% to 7.8% (United Nations System in Cuba, 2026; MINSAP, 2025).

Communicable diseases have als o increased, with tuberculosis rising from 5.7 to 12.2 per 100,000 inhabitants, syphilis from 38.1 to 72.3, and hepatitis A from 3.4 to 25.9 per 100,000 inhabitants (United Nations System in Cuba, 2026).
